name: Foot powder
lead: Foot powder is a dusting powder applied to the feet and sometimes inside shoes to absorb moisture and reduce odour, and some formulations contain antifungal or deodorant agents. It is used in grooming routines to manage foot sweat and odour.

Evidence is mostly indirect. A 1974 report from a swimming bath found that supplying foot powder sachets to bathers coincided with a fall in tinea pedis incidence,[2] and a skin-product study included a foot powder among four products tested for effects on the skin microbiome.[1] Contact allergy to an antimicrobial ingredient in one deodorant foot powder has been reported.[3]

paras: Foot odour is generally attributed to sweat and bacterial breakdown of skin, and general references list foot hygiene, dry socks, medicated insoles and foot powder among prevention measures.[6] Powders are also used in the management of fungal infections of the feet; a podiatry review notes that infected shoes and socks can act as reservoirs for reinfection, so sanitising footwear is discussed alongside treatment.[4]
A 1975 case report described two people with allergic contact dermatitis to the antimicrobial Irgasan, one from a deodorant foot powder.[3]

In a 1974 study of a public swimming pool, random samples of bathers were examined before and after individual foot powder sachets were provided; over three and a half years overall tinea pedis incidence fell from 8.5% to 2.1%, and in adult males from 21.5% to 6.9%.[2] The study was uncontrolled by modern standards. A 2019 study of 11 volunteers over nine weeks tested four products including a foot powder and examined skin chemistry and microbial diversity; its clearest reported change followed halting deodorant use.[1] A 1960 paper describes clinical trials of a commercial foot powder.[5] No trial specifically measuring cosmetic foot odour was found.

timeline.event: A US Army medical bulletin reports a new foot powder to prevent cold injuries.[7]
Clinical trials of a foot powder are reported in a podiatry journal.[5]
Swimming-bath study links foot powder sachets to lower tinea pedis incidence.[2]

lore.intro: Foot powder is discussed in grooming circles as a simple fix for sweaty feet and shoe odour.

claims.claim: Foot powder keeps feet dry and cuts odour
claims.believers: Users say a dusting before socks reduces dampness and smell through the day.
claims.experts: General references list foot powder among odour-prevention measures,[6] but no trial measuring odour outcomes was found.

card.summary: Dusting powder for sweaty feet; sensible and cheap, but evidence is indirect.
card.note: Rare contact allergy to some deodorant ingredients reported.

quick.overview:
Foot powder is applied to feet or shoes to absorb moisture and reduce odour. Some products add antifungal or deodorant agents.

A 1974 swimming-bath report linked powder sachets to fewer athlete's foot cases, but no trial of cosmetic odour control was found.
quick.mechanism: Powders absorb sweat; odour is attributed to bacteria breaking down sweat and dead skin.
quick.risks: Contact allergy to an antimicrobial ingredient in one deodorant foot powder has been reported.
